en: And sent him to the six uncles.
“Abyke, Kobosh—two of my uncles;
Chyibyt, Kochkor—four of my uncles;
Adybai, Kolbai—six of my uncles;
The supports left by my father,
All forty companions,
Their elders, led by Kyrgyl—
My khan father who has gone to Judgment Day,
Tell them to come, not one left behind!
For my dear uncle Baimyrza,
Tell them to cast a handful of earth,
Tell them to act as kin!
Tell them to gather the people,
Tell them to serve with all their strength!
If their kinship is true,
Tell them to stand beneath the banner,
Tell them to perform this service!
Five groups of nine, each headed by a mare,
Let us boil for his burial-day feast;
Vast riches and yellow gold
Let us spread out for his funeral.
Six hundred gifts, headed by a horse,
Let us pledge for his absolution rite,
Of the religious elders and mullahs
Thus easing their minds.
Saying, ‘This Baimyrza has died,’
Saying, ‘He has seen Judgment Day,’
When we bury this rich man,
Let us devise what no one else could imagine,
Hold a great, tumultuous feast,
Raise dust along the dark road,
Prepare the swiftest horses,
Arrange strong, steadfast cheering,
Send them racing far away;
Of Baimyrza's countless horses
Let us set aside half,
Put them up as the race prizes!
He was an elder of ninety-five;
Let us honor him in this way.
Let us stand beneath the banner,
Make his fame known to the great multitude,
Raise a great stir,
And bid him farewell with this!
Yellow-mottled Andijan cloth with a thick weft,
Precious black-mottled cloth from Bukhara—
Let us gather them for his funeral,
Let us serve him in this way.
Does not a mortal human die?
Do not his friends and companions bury him?
Does not a living soul go on with life!
In Temir Khan's city,
Growing up in exile,
Let them see the orphan's face;
Let my six uncles come here.
Our father was of the same nest,
If I have behaved rashly,
Let me submit to what is right.
Let my six uncles come to me;
I will offer my mother as a gift.
At Baimyrza's great funeral,
Tell them to take their place at that great funeral.
Go and tell uncles Abyke and Kobosh,
Tell them to act as brothers.
From my horses I will offer
A steed such as Taitoru;
As compensation I will offer
My elder uncle Bakai.
I will offer without holding back
My own twelve-year-old life!
Say these are Semetey's pure, honest intentions.
Say that, when he reached ninety years,
This is the funeral feast of Baimyrza, departed from this world!
Let the kinsmen gather in a crowd,
Tell them to cast the earth;
A set of nine headed by a camel,
Tell them to take as their funeral gift!
For Baimyrza's funeral
I will give more than other peoples do.
With its lower lip drooping,
Its two humps standing proudly,
I will give a burden-bearing camel.
I will give red gold for the mourning gifts;
I will give abundant riches.
Sarykan with eyes like bowls,
My sultan uncle, listen!
If he speaks against you and uses force,
If my khan uncle acts against you,
For Baimyrza's funeral service
I will seize his mares by force,
I will bind his giants;
If he comes near then,
I will strike and scatter his brains!
If I truly set to it, I will drive out—
Let them not be late.
If they delay through quarreling,
Let them prepare a place to quarrel;
Let not a single one arrive late.
Let them not put on weighty airs.
If they throw their weight about and use force,
Let them prepare the place for a lance fight!
This is the greeting I send;
Uncle Sary, listen carefully!
Say it to my six uncles' faces.
Say it to the slave Shuutu's face,
Say it among the forty companions!
Strong-armed Baichoro,
The faithful support left by my father—
Tell such a hero.
Kyrgylchal, head of the forty,
Tell that unbeliever who disrupts the people.
Tell Yraman's Yrchuul;
Tell the diviner, Kara Tolok.
Tell the elders among the clans;
Tell all forty companions!
Abyke, who finds wise counsel,
Was a wise and heroic kinsman;
My uncle Kobosh moved heavily and grandly,
My holy sage who has seen much,
My elder, born to bring people good fortune!
Kobosh and Kyrgylchal
Were dogs of evil temper;
If they speak unrestrained words,
Do not stoop to that dog's level.
Hey, Uncle Sary Khan!
If you give way, you will earn a bad name.
To Abyke and Kobosh
You are going as an envoy;
Uncle, I entrust this to you now!”
Then Sary Khan,
Clad in blue iron armor,
Springing like a blue tiger,
Girding on his cutting sword,
Readying all his weapons,
Like a cloud in the sky,
Moving back and forth,
Preparing his arms for war,
Had surpassingly eloquent speech,
Had eyes like bowls.
Had you seen your uncle Sary,
Anyone who came before him
Would suddenly start in fright,
His heart sorely troubled;
Seen from behind,
He looked like a mighty mountain.
Readying his lacquered spear,
Girding his battle-axe slantwise,
Hanging at one side—
A devastating bow, smooth arrowheads,
Your uncle Sary Khan
Set the world talking.
A helmet of blue iron
Was fitted over his head.
If you ask about your uncle,
He had a warrior's frame and a broad chest;
His coat was of blue iron.
If seven worlds of enemies came,
He would charge alone into their midst.
The mount beneath him—
The peerless courser Tuuchunak,
A Karabair courser,
With sieve-like lungs and brass forelegs,
Never tiring when ridden on reconnaissance,
Never ailing when ridden in the rear guard,
With hoe-like hooves and a broad rump,
Well-formed Tuuchunak.
Unless a bullet struck him,
Unless untimely death overtook him,
He would not falter when ridden into battle,
The otherworldly courser Tuuchunak.
The mount beneath him,
His swift Tuuchunak,
Leaving the royal camp behind,
Looming like a mighty mountain,
He rode with splendid bearing,
Knotting the horse's long tail firmly,
Venom pouring from his face,
Mighty in strength, fierce in countenance,
A dear soul whose valor was precious.
Once a charcoal burner, blackened with soot,
He had joined Semetey,
All his misfortunes were dispelled,
He became a giant, sultan of the Argyn.
Now he went as an intermediary.
Urging the horse across the grassy mountain slopes,
When he reached the rolling hills,
He let the reins go free.
Along broad Urbus,
Where Abyke and Kobosh stayed,
Sary Khan with eyes like bowls
Came riding hard.
Look at the trench they had dug,
Look at the seething army,
Look at the white banner,
Look at the shouting tumult!
Mist settled in corners,
The people gathered and armed themselves,
Swaying in ranks along the edge,
Khan Kobosh's royal camp
Was surrounded by a mass of troops, surging.
A red banner mottled with gray,
Many cries of “Oh!” and a tumult,
A white-mottled pennon, a red banner,
Shrill shouts and a tumult.
Marksmen crouched,
Lancers stood stiffly erect,
Axemen made ready;
Abyke and Kobosh's
Great army was preparing.
There were seven banners,
An army that bent the earth,
Their assembled forces were vast.
Abyke and Kobosh were not alone:
There were troops from every region,
So many they bent the earth.
When Semetey had gone to Bukhara,
He who dwelt in Eki-Kemin,
Who tethered a pair of black horses,
Who sowed his rice as an autumn crop,
The barnyard grass from his rice fields
He tied up for his horse,
Who sharpened his tongue,
Who spoke eloquently before the khan,
Who gathered harriers and made them hunting birds,
Who gathered mixed folk and made them a people,
Who made the dark forest his livestock,
Who made a dark cave his home—
The hero Urbu, son of bald Eybit—
Abyke, Kobosh, the six villains,
Had sent word to Urbu,
Gathered Urbu's army,
And assembled it in Talas.
He who dwelt in Sary-Arka,
Called a weighty, formidable hero,
Who husked his millet, stones and all,
Who praised his wife like a maiden,
Whose lattice walls were made of wood,
Aidarkan's hero Kokcho,
Kokcho's son Umotoy—
Stinking sour milk and blue-green dried curds—
From the shouting Kazakhs,
They had brought Umotoy's army;
The villains Abyke and Kobosh
Had assembled it.
Khans who would act with hostility,
Men who would fire shots,
They had gathered them all.
Golden-crowned Muzburchak,
Muzburchak's son Buyanbek—
Saying, “Avenge your father,”
“Manas's orphan son—
Offer him as a sacrifice,”
They had brought him there.
His son Chynkozho,
Kozho, whose deeds too were vigorous,
Saying, “Manas's orphan son
I will offer as a sacrifice,
